title: The 60-Day Wait: Why a Major Retail Listing Can Leave a Food Producer Short on Cash
linkedin:
A major supermarket listing is meant to be the moment a food producer's business stops feeling fragile. National shelf space, a real purchase order, validation a growing brand rarely gets anywhere else.

For a lot of producers, it's also the moment cash gets tightest.

The purchase order confirms revenue is coming. It doesn't confirm when. Major retailers typically pay forty five to ninety days from invoice, and that invoice usually can't be raised until stock has cleared the retailer's own distribution centre and quality checks.

Meanwhile the producer's own costs, ingredients, packaging, contract labour, freight, are mostly paid before the product even leaves the factory floor. By the time payment lands, ninety to a hundred and twenty days can have passed since the ingredients were first ordered.

Here's the part that catches people off guard. A bigger order doesn't fix this. It usually makes it worse. A reorder often lands while the first invoice is still weeks from being paid, meaning a second production run needs funding before the first one has returned any cash at all.

This is how a food producer can show healthy revenue growth and solid gross margin, and still struggle to make payroll. It's not a profitability problem. It's a timing problem that compounds every time the order book grows.

The producers who manage it well model the cash conversion cycle for each retail relationship before accepting the volume, then size the first order, supplier terms and any bridging finance around that number rather than around optimism.

Full piece on the ProfitPulse blog.
